FACULTY SENATE OFFICE 224 PASTORE HALL, 51 LOWER COLLEGE ROAD, KINGSTON, RI 02881 USA, P: 401.874.2616 Faculty Senate Resolution 2024-2025-03 Faculty Senate Meeting of January 23, 2025 Resolution on the Implementation of Honors Contracts WHEREAS, following considerable self-study and significant input from external experts, the URI Honors Program has proposed the use of honors contracts at URI.
Honors contracts are formal agreements, facilitated by an honors program, between a student and instructor.
They allow students and instructors to enhance non-honors courses to an honors level through additional learner-directed work tailored to the “broader, deeper, and more complex” learning experiences advocated by the National Collegiate Honors Council (NCHC); and WHEREAS, contracts are recognized by over 60% of honors programs in the USA, where they foster community and ownership by enhancing the educational process and commitment to the programs’ success.
For example, work at the University Honors Program at the University of Kansas shows that honors contracts act as far more than stopgaps to address honors course shortages.

They can “facilitate access to honors, increases completion, democratize key aspects of the honors experience, provide students with structured avenues for building relationships with faculty members, and empower students to own their educational experiences”; and WHEREAS, honors contracts may be best understood as a form of an independent study, entered into voluntarily by both students and faculty, with a contract defining outcomes, deadlines, and assessment definitions for additional work related to the course materials; and WHEREAS, honors contracts provide flexibility for students to align their education with their interests and goals.
They also allow programs to meet student needs when student/faculty constraints or funding limitations preclude offering stand-alone honors courses that fit student interests and needs; and WHEREAS, Contracts provide an extra measure of curricular flexibility at institutions such as ours that are not able to field enough faculty, cannot provide an adequate number of honors courses, or do not have a large enough student body to fill honors sections.

Contracts can fill the gap and provide opportunities for the self-guided intellectual growth of students; NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Faculty Senate of the University of Rhode Island calls for implementation of the following Honors Contracts Proposal.
This includes making the

recommended changes to the University Catalog and to the eCampus system used by Enrollment Services; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the Honors Program is called upon to reflect these changes on their website and in all other promotional and outreach materials promulgated by the Program. The Program is also called upon to review Chapter 8 of the University Manual (Academic Regulations, Honors Program) in light of the Contracts Proposal and bring any recommended changes to the Faculty Senate expeditiously; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the authority to offer Honors Contracts enabled by this resolution shall not extend beyond the Fall 2025 semester; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that no instructor may participate in more than three Honors Contracts in a single semester. Adopted this 23rd day of January, 2025. ____________________________________________________________ T heodore Walls, URI Faculty Senate President

To stand out in a crowded market, programs often seek accreditation from prestigious bodies like AACSB, AMBA, or EQUIS and aim to secure favorable rankings from notable publications.
Many programs also forge partnerships with businesses and other organizations to help in curriculum development, provide real-world learning opportunities, and facilitate networking and job placements for graduates.

Recent trends in MSM programs include an increased emphasis on technology and analytics to integrate digital technologies in business, a focus on sustainability and social responsibility reflecting broader societal concerns, and more customizable and flexible learning paths to attract a diverse student body with varying needs and career goals.
Overall, the market for MSM programs remains robust, driven by their relevance, accessibility, and adaptability to market needs and educational technologies, though programs must continuously innovate and adapt to remain competitive.

Existing Language 8.59.10 Assessment of student learning outcomes shall be coordinated by the Learning Outcomes Oversight Committee (LOOC; see 5.84.10 – 5.84.13) in cooperation with the Assistant Director of Student Learning, Outcomes Assessment and Accreditation (see 2.22.21).
The following policies shall apply to this process: 8.59.11 Academic Program Engagement.

All undergraduate, professional, and graduate academic programs, including General Education, shall be actively engaged in student learning outcomes assessment as evidenced by, but not limited to: a) Published student learning outcomes that are clear statements of what students are expected to gain, achieve, demonstrate, or know at the completion of the academic program.
These student learning outcomes shall be published on the program’s website as well as on the website for the Office of Student Learning, Outcomes Assessment, and Accreditation (SLOAA).
These student learning outcomes shall be periodically reviewed by the academic program for ongoing relevance. b) A plan of student learning outcomes assessment that is endorsed by the program’s faculty.
Plans should include a regular and predictable cycle for collecting and analyzing assessment data, for discussing curricular and programmatic changes, for implementing interventions, and for re-assessing the impact of implemented changes.

To: URI Faculty Senate From: Peter Paton: Chair – Joint Classroom Steering Committee (JCSC) Members: Katie Babula, Keith Brown, Katherine Kittredge, Dean Libutti, Lenore Martin, Ann Morrissey, Janie Palm, David Porter, Ken Sisson, Leon Theim, Ryan Trimm, Jeff Ulricksen.
Date: 18 March 2022 Subject: Summary of JCSC allocations this year The JCSC has funds allocated annual for all General Assignment Classrooms on the Kingston campus.
The committee has allocated $400,000 annually for upgrades to Audio-visual technology and $300,000 for basic infrastructure within classrooms (e.g., chairs, tables, lecterns, blinds), so excludes big ticket items such as HVAC systems (which we are aware have issues in buildings but are beyond the committee).
The committee has a list of when all the AV technology in GAC classrooms has last been updated, and we try to upgrade equipment ~5 years.
Specific upgrades this year: Beaupre Projectors: Replace the outdated projectors in both Beaupre Lecture Halls with laser projectors $29,450 Ranger Hall Mac Minis Note- These new GACs will come online Fall 22- Summary: There are 11 GACs going online in Ranger hall as part of finishing the top 2 floors of the building.

On the project, classroom computers were listed as OFE (owner furnished equipment). $9,867 Computer upgrades: Computer upgrades for all the auditoria on campus along with other outdated machines in GAC classrooms $28,412.55 Active Learning Lite Classroom Quinn rms 214, 211, 209, Chafee 235, 244, 235, 251: Upgrade flat panel displays; Purchase 14 projectors as backup stock to replace projectors that cease to function: $69,834 Replace projection screens in Avedisian 170 and Ballentine 115. $10,448 Swan Hall Projector Replacement (16 Rooms) Summary: As we continue to work towards changing over all campus projectors to lasers (instead of lamps) swapping the entire buildings remaining lamp-based projectors out would be a bulk cost savings move.

It’s especially helpful in these spaces as newer projectors will always be brighter and all of Swan classrooms have windows which face towards the projected displays. $64,050 Lectern Furniture Update Summary: This project would allow for changing out the older solid wood lecterns in Chafee (2nd floor), Quinn (2nd floor), and Swan to the newer style lecterns that were put in place for the 21C project and in Bliss and Fascitelli Engineering building.
The metal lecterns allow for better airflow and

heat regulation of systems as well as offer ADA height adjustment to the primary instructor work surface. $116,050 AirMedia Wireless Presentation Device Updates Summary: We have various versions of the Crestron wireless presentation device deployed in classrooms based upon their installation year. Due to a Crestron program change, this means, from mobile devices, not all rooms are capable of fully mirroring device screens. This also results in there being 2 different Apps that instructors must know which one is the correct one to use with the device. Phasing out these older units eliminates this confusion and broadens system capability for faculty. This affects roughly 50 rooms. $51,396.40 Holdover Bill from FY 21: $11,683.40 Total spending to date: $391,191.13 Infrastructure fund: $300,000 annual allocation; We acquired 600 Learn2 chairs for 16 classrooms in Swan Hall (excluding Auditorium) using this year’s funds – those chairs were acquired for this academic year and the cost was $285,000. We also bought 16 accessible tables with adjustable height surfaces for the 16 classrooms in Swan Hall with remaining funds to accommodate students with disabilities for $15,000. Ken Sisson stated this was a problem for all classrooms on campus and there really needs to be greater efforts to provide infrastructure for students with disabilities.

Report from Faculty Senate Executive Committee March 24, 2022 Standing Committee Membership Rationale: With changes in apportionment for AY 22-23 the Senate will increase by 10 Senators.
To enable all Senators to serve on a standing committee, as well as provide flexibility in the Committees, the capped number of members per committee should change to identify only the minimum number of members.
Motion: Adjust all membership numbers for standing committees to indicate minimum number of members only.
Appendix C: BYLAWS 4.13 Each committee shall be comprise d of four to six or more faculty members, one of whom shall serve as chairperson, and two students, one undergraduate and one graduate student.
The faculty members of standing committees shall serve for three-year terms on a staggered basis from the time of their approval until the first meeting of the Senate in the fall three years afterwards.
Committee chairs shall serve for two years in that capacity.
Student members shall serve for one year and shall be eligible for appointment to a second term.
Students shall be appointed, respectively, by the Student Senate and by the Graduate Student Association.

Committee chairs or the Faculty Senate Executive Committee may request that the University administration make available those administrators and/or staff members whose expertise is aligned with the work of the committees to act as liaisons to committees as needed.
Administrator and/or staff liaisons may advise committee members regarding the work of the committee but shall not be considered committee members.
The Executive Committee or committee chairs may also ask faculty who are not Senate members to serve as non-voting advisors to standing committees as needed. #17-18-11, #17-18-17, #20-21-14 4.20 The Curriculum and Standards Committee shall comprise six or more faculty members one of whom serves as the chairperson of the General Education committee.
The chair of the General Education Committee shall be appointed from the members of the committee.
The committee shall consider and make recommendations to the Faculty Senate on the items specifically assigned to it (see By-laws 4.21 to 4.25).
The committee shall meet at least once a month and present reports to the Faculty Senate as often as necessary.

Joint meetings of the Curriculum and Standards and General Education curriculum committees shall occur early fall and late spring to review and calibrate standards for course review. #17-18-12, #20-21-14

4.27 The General Education Committee shall comprise six or more members, one of whom is the chair of the Curriculum and Standards committee.
The committee shall study and make recommendations on the establishment, modification or abolition of General Education requirements for graduation to be applicable to degree candidates; consider new and existing courses proposed for general education; evaluate the effectiveness of the general education program; maintain liaison with the University administration for effective implementation of approved recommendations; and cooperate closely with the Director of General Education (see University Manual section 8.20.30).
The Curriculum and Standards Committee and the General Education Committee shall maintain consistent standards by which courses are reviewed. #17-18-12, #20-21-14, #21-22-6 4.28 The Academic Calendar Committee shall comprise four or more members.

The committee shall study the University Calendar for fall, winter, spring, and summer session semesters as prepared by Enrollment Services in accordance with University Manual passages 8.70.10 and 8.70.61, respectively, report it to the Faculty Senate by December 1; study the calendar for the fully-online accelerated program developed in accordance with University Manual passage 8.70.72 and present the calendar to the Faculty Senate by March 1 of the year preceding the one during which the calendar is to become effective; carry out all other functions assigned to it by University Manual passages 8.70.10-75; examine, cooperatively with the Graduate Council, such academic matters as may affect jointly the two committees; consider such calendar matters as may be referred to it by the Senate or its Executive Committee, and study, on its own accord, desirable changes in the University Calendar; review any proposed change in the approved calendar originating outside the committee as well as any amendments attached by the Faculty Senate to a calendar proposal prior to Faculty Senate adoption of the calendar in its final form except that, if the Senate Executive Committee declares an emergency situation prior to the Faculty Senate meeting at which calendar proposals are to be considered, a calendar proposal amended on the Senate floor may be approved at the meeting during which the proposal has first been introduced by the full committee. #17-18-12, #19-20-16, #20-21-14, #21-22-6 4.30 The Teaching, Advising, and Assessment Committee shall comprise five or more faculty members, and consider and make recommendations to the Faculty Senate on the items specifically assigned to it (see By-laws 4.31-4.34).

The Committee shall study and make recommendations to the Faculty Senate (or return the matters unapproved, with comments, to the units from which they originated) on the following matters referred to it by the various colleges, schools, the Faculty Senate or its Executive Committee, the Administration, or from another authoritative source, or taken up by the Committee on its own initiative: 4.40 The Committee for Research and Creative Activities (henceforth referred to as the “full committee”) shall consist of faculty and students active, experienced, or concerned with various aspects of research, creative, and scholarly efforts at URI.
The full committee shall serve as the representative voice of the university community in all matters related to research, creative, and scholarly activities and shall seek to improve the environment for research at URI in all ways possible.
The full committee shall also comprise two subcommittees, the Competitive Grants

Subcommittee and the Center Review Subcommittee.
